items.title: Our Changing Climate: Causes, Effects, and Solutions
items.zh: 正在变化的气候：原因、影响与对策
items.summary: 温室效应是怎么回事、证据从哪里来、对天气、海洋、农业和健康有什么影响，以及国家、企业和个人分别能做什么。高中阶段的科学与社会类高频词。
paras: Climate change is one of the most discussed issues of our time. It appears in news headlines, political debates, school lessons, and conversations at the dinner table. Yet many people still feel confused about it. What exactly is happening? How do scientists know? How serious is it? And can anything be done? This article aims to answer these questions clearly, using the evidence that scientists have collected over many decades.
Weather and climate

First, it is important to understand the difference between weather and climate. Weather describes the conditions in a particular place over a short period of time: today's temperature, tomorrow's rain, this week's storm. Climate describes the average weather patterns in a region over a long period, usually thirty years or more. A single cold winter does not disprove climate change, just as a single hot summer does not prove it. Scientists look at long-term trends across the whole planet.
The greenhouse effect

Life on Earth depends on something called the greenhouse effect. Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface of the Earth. The Earth then releases some of this energy back toward space as heat. Certain gases in the atmosphere, called greenhouse gases, absorb part of this heat and send it back toward the surface, a little like the glass walls of a greenhouse that keep plants warm. The most important greenhouse gases are water vapor, carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide.

Without the greenhouse effect, the average temperature on Earth would be about minus eighteen degrees Celsius, far too cold for most life. So the greenhouse effect itself is natural and necessary. The problem is that human activities have been increasing the amount of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, especially carbon dioxide. As a result, more heat is trapped in the atmosphere, and the planet is getting warmer.
Where do the extra gases come from?

The main source of extra carbon dioxide is the burning of fossil fuels: coal, oil, and natural gas. These fuels were formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient plants and animals, and they contain large amounts of carbon. When we burn them to generate electricity, power factories, heat buildings, and run cars, trucks, ships, and planes, that carbon is released into the air as carbon dioxide.

Other human activities also contribute. Cutting down forests, known as deforestation, removes trees that would otherwise absorb carbon dioxide. Agriculture produces large amounts of methane, especially from cattle and rice fields. Methane is released from landfills, where garbage breaks down, and from leaks in oil and gas systems. Although there is much less methane than carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, it is a far more powerful greenhouse gas in the short term.
The evidence
How do scientists know that the climate is changing, and that humans are responsible? The evidence comes from many independent sources.

Direct measurements. Scientists have been measuring carbon dioxide in the air since 1958, at an observatory on a mountain in Hawaii. In 1958, the level was about 315 parts per million. Today, it is over 420 parts per million, the highest level in at least eight hundred thousand years.

Temperature records. Thousands of weather stations, ships, buoys, and satellites measure temperatures around the world. It is estimated that global temperatures have risen by about 1.2 degrees Celsius since the late 1800s. That may not sound like much, but it is an average over the entire planet, including the oceans. Most of the warmest years ever recorded have occurred in the last decade.

Ice cores. In Antarctica and Greenland, scientists drill deep into the ice and remove long cylinders called ice cores. The ice contains tiny bubbles of ancient air, which reveal the composition of the atmosphere hundreds of thousands of years ago. These records show a close connection between carbon dioxide levels and temperature throughout Earth's history.

Physical changes. Glaciers around the world are shrinking. Arctic sea ice has declined significantly since satellite measurements began in the late 1970s. Sea levels are rising, partly because melting ice adds water to the oceans, and partly because water expands as it warms. Spring is arriving earlier in many regions, and many plant and animal species are moving toward the poles or to higher altitudes.

Scientific organizations around the world, including national academies of science and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, have concluded that human activities are the main cause of the warming observed since the mid-twentieth century.
The effects
A warmer planet affects almost every part of the natural world and human society.

Extreme weather. Warmer air can hold more water vapor, which can lead to heavier rainfall and more serious floods in some areas. At the same time, higher temperatures increase evaporation, making droughts more severe in other areas. Heat waves are becoming more frequent and more intense. Many regions, including the western United States, Australia, and southern Europe, have experienced longer and more destructive wildfire seasons.

Rising seas. Sea levels have risen by more than twenty centimeters since 1900, and the rate is increasing. If emissions continue to rise, sea levels will rise even faster. This threatens coastal cities, islands, and farmland. Low-lying countries and large coastal cities such as Miami, Jakarta, and Shanghai face serious risks from flooding and storm surges.

Oceans. The oceans have absorbed a large share of the extra heat and about a quarter of the extra carbon dioxide. This has protected us from even greater warming, but it has a cost. When carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater, it makes the water more acidic, which harms coral reefs and shellfish. Warmer water also causes coral bleaching, in which corals lose the colorful algae they depend on.

Food and water. Changes in temperature and rainfall affect where and how crops can grow. Some northern regions may benefit from longer growing seasons, but many important farming regions face more heat stress, drought, and unpredictable weather. Mountain glaciers provide water for hundreds of millions of people, and as they shrink, water supplies become less reliable.

Health. Heat waves are dangerous, especially for older people, young children, and outdoor workers. Changing climates also allow diseases carried by mosquitoes, such as malaria and dengue fever, to spread to new areas. Air pollution from burning fossil fuels and from wildfires causes millions of early deaths every year.

Unequal impacts. The people who are most affected by climate change are often those who have contributed least to it. Poorer countries and communities usually have fewer resources to protect themselves from floods, droughts, and heat. This raises important questions of fairness and responsibility.
What can be done?

The good news is that many solutions already exist, and many of them are becoming cheaper every year. Experts usually divide the solutions into two categories: mitigation, which means reducing emissions to slow climate change, and adaptation, which means preparing for the changes that are already happening.

Clean energy. The most important step is to replace fossil fuels with low-carbon sources of energy. The cost of solar panels has fallen by around ninety percent in the last decade, and wind power has also become much cheaper. In many parts of the world, building new solar or wind farms is now cheaper than building new coal power plants. Other low-carbon sources include hydroelectric power, geothermal energy, and nuclear power, although each of these has its own advantages and disadvantages.

Electric transportation. Transportation is a major source of emissions. Electric vehicles produce no exhaust emissions, and when they are charged with clean electricity, their overall emissions are much lower than those of gasoline cars. Sales of electric cars have grown rapidly. Public transportation, cycling, and walking also play important roles, especially in cities.

Efficiency. Using less energy to do the same job is often the cheapest way to reduce emissions. Better insulation in buildings, efficient heating and cooling systems such as heat pumps, LED lighting, and more efficient industrial processes all help.
Protecting nature. Forests, wetlands, and grasslands store huge amounts of carbon. Protecting existing forests and restoring damaged ecosystems can both reduce emissions and protect biodiversity.

Adaptation. Even if emissions fell sharply tomorrow, some further warming is unavoidable. Communities need to adapt by building stronger flood defenses, developing crops that can survive drought, improving early warning systems for extreme weather, and designing cities that stay cooler in summer, for example by planting trees and using light-colored roofs.
The role of governments, businesses, and individuals

Governments need to act quickly. They can set targets for reducing emissions, invest in clean energy and public transportation, put a price on carbon so that polluters pay for the damage they cause, and create rules for cleaner cars and buildings. In 2015, almost every country in the world signed the Paris Agreement, in which they agreed to try to limit warming to well below two degrees Celsius, and ideally to 1.5 degrees. However, many countries' current plans are not yet strong enough to meet these goals.

Businesses also have a major role. Companies can switch to renewable energy, make their products more efficient, reduce waste, and build cleaner supply chains. Many large companies have announced goals to reach "net zero" emissions, although critics point out that some of these promises are vague or depend too much on uncertain technologies.

What about individuals? Some people argue that individual actions are too small to matter compared to the actions of governments and large companies. Others argue that individual choices add up, and that they send important signals to businesses and politicians. Most experts believe that both are important. Here are some of the actions that have the biggest impact for individuals in wealthy countries: using public transportation, cycling, or electric vehicles instead of gasoline cars; flying less, especially long-distance flights; improving the energy efficiency of your home; eating less red meat; reducing food waste; and supporting policies and leaders that take climate change seriously.

Talking about climate change in your community, at school, or at work also matters. Studies show that many people care about climate change but rarely discuss it, so they assume others do not care. Simply talking about it can help change that.
A closer look: life in a hotter city

To understand what these changes mean in daily life, consider a city like Phoenix, Arizona, or the inland areas of Southern California. Summers there have always been hot, but the number of days above one hundred degrees Fahrenheit has increased, and nights are not cooling down as much as they used to. This matters because the human body needs cooler nights to recover from daytime heat. Outdoor workers, such as construction crews, farm workers, delivery drivers, and people who work in warehouse yards, are especially at risk. Many employers now schedule heavy work for early morning, provide shade and water, and train workers to recognize the signs of heat exhaustion, such as dizziness, headache, and confusion. Cities are planting more trees, painting roofs white, and opening cooling centers where people without air conditioning can rest. These are examples of adaptation in action. They do not stop climate change, but they help people stay safe while the world works on reducing emissions.
Reasons for hope

It is easy to feel overwhelmed or hopeless about climate change. The problem is enormous, and the news can be frightening. But there are real reasons for hope. Clean energy technologies have improved faster than almost anyone predicted. In many countries, emissions have already started to fall while the economy continues to grow. Young people around the world have become powerful voices for action. And history shows that humans can solve large global problems when they work together. In the 1980s, countries agreed to ban chemicals that were destroying the ozone layer, and today the ozone layer is slowly recovering.

Every fraction of a degree of warming that we prevent matters. A world that is 1.5 degrees warmer is significantly safer than a world that is two degrees warmer, which in turn is far safer than a world that is three degrees warmer. The future is not yet written. The choices made in the next few decades, by governments, businesses, and each of us, will shape the planet for centuries to come.

items.title: Fake News and How to Think Clearly
items.summary: 为什么假消息比真消息传得快、算法和"信息茧房"怎么影响我们、常见的误导手法，以及判断一条消息是否可信的实用步骤。高中阶段媒体素养和批判性思维的高频词。
paras: A few years ago, a dramatic photo spread quickly across social media. It showed a shark swimming on a flooded highway during a hurricane. Thousands of people shared it with comments like "Unbelievable!" and "Stay safe, everyone!" There was only one problem: the photo was fake. Someone had taken a real photo of a shark from a nature magazine and digitally placed it on a picture of a flooded road. Remarkably, the same fake image has appeared again during almost every major hurricane since then.

The shark photo is harmless and a little funny. But false information is not always harmless. False health claims can lead people to take dangerous treatments or avoid useful ones. Rumors can damage people's reputations and even lead to violence. False stories about elections can reduce trust in democracy. In a world where anyone can publish anything to millions of people in seconds, the ability to tell truth from falsehood has become an essential life skill.
What is "fake news"?

The term "fake news" is used in many different ways, and some experts prefer more precise terms. Misinformation is false or misleading information that is shared without the intention to deceive. For example, your aunt might share a false health tip because she genuinely believes it will help people. Disinformation is false information that is created and spread deliberately to deceive, often for political or financial reasons. And propaganda is information, true or false, that is designed to promote a particular political cause or point of view, usually by appealing to emotions rather than reason.

There is also a large gray area. A story might contain accurate facts but present them in a misleading way. A real photo might be shared with a false description. A true quote might be taken out of context so that it appears to mean something completely different. These subtle forms of manipulation are often harder to recognize than obvious lies.
Why false information spreads so fast

In 2018, researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology published a major study of news stories shared on Twitter over more than ten years. Researchers found that false news spread significantly faster than true news. False stories were about seventy percent more likely to be shared than true ones, and they reached people much more quickly. Interestingly, the researchers found that this was not mainly caused by automated accounts, known as bots. It was caused by real people.

Why do people share false stories more than true ones? One reason is novelty. False stories are often more surprising than true ones, because they are not limited by reality. Our brains are naturally attracted to new and surprising information. Another reason is emotion. False stories often provoke strong emotions such as anger, fear, or disgust. When we feel a strong emotion, we are more likely to react quickly and share something without thinking carefully.

Social media platforms also play a role. Most platforms use algorithms, which are computer programs that decide what content to show each user. These algorithms are often designed to maximize "engagement," meaning likes, comments, shares, and time spent on the platform. Unfortunately, content that makes people angry or shocked tends to generate a lot of engagement, so the algorithm may show it to even more people.
Filter bubbles and echo chambers

Algorithms also learn what we like and show us more of it. If you often watch videos about a particular topic or click on stories with a particular political viewpoint, you will probably see more and more content of that kind. Over time, this can create what is called a filter bubble: a personal information environment in which you mainly see ideas that match what you already believe.

Similarly, people tend to follow and interact with others who share their opinions. This can create an echo chamber, in which the same ideas are repeated and reinforced, while different views are rarely heard or are presented only in their most extreme forms. In an echo chamber, it can seem as if "everyone" agrees with you, and people who disagree can seem not just wrong but foolish or evil.

Researchers continue to debate how strong these effects are. Some studies suggest that most people actually see a fairly wide range of views online. But it is clear that our information environment is shaped by our own choices and by the algorithms of the platforms we use, and that it is worth making an effort to see different perspectives.
Our brains are part of the problem

It is easy to assume that only other people fall for false information. But psychological research shows that all of us have mental shortcuts, called cognitive biases, that can lead us to believe things that are not true.

Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, notice, and remember information that confirms what we already believe, and to ignore or dismiss information that contradicts it. If you already dislike a politician, you will be much more likely to believe a negative story about them without checking it.

The illusory truth effect means that when we hear a statement many times, we start to believe it is true, even if we initially knew it was false. Repetition creates familiarity, and familiarity feels like truth. This is one reason why false claims that are repeated again and again can become widely believed.

The bandwagon effect is the tendency to believe or do something because many other people do. When we see that a post has been shared a hundred thousand times, we may assume it must be true. However, popularity is not evidence.
Being aware of these biases does not make us immune to them, but it can help us slow down and think more carefully, especially when a story makes us feel strongly.
Common tricks of misleading content
People who create misleading content often use the same techniques. Learning to recognize them is an important defense.

Emotional headlines. Headlines written in capital letters, with many exclamation marks, or with phrases such as "You won't believe..." or "What they don't want you to know" are designed to make you click and share, not to inform you.

Missing sources. A claim such as "Scientists say..." or "A study found..." without saying which scientists or which study should make you suspicious. Reliable reporting usually tells you where the information comes from, so that you can check it yourself.

Out-of-context images. A real photo or video from one event can be presented as if it shows a different event. The video was said to show a recent flood in one country, but it was actually filmed years earlier in another country. A quick reverse image search can often reveal the original source.

Manipulated media. Photos can be edited, and increasingly, artificial intelligence can be used to create realistic fake images, audio, and video, sometimes called deepfakes. The photo might have been edited. Look for strange details, such as unusual hands, unnatural lighting, or text that does not make sense.

Misleading statistics. Numbers can be presented in a way that is technically true but misleading. For example, "Crime rose by one hundred percent!" sounds dramatic, but if the number went from two incidents to four in a small town, it does not mean much. Always ask: compared to what? Over what period? How big was the sample?
Fake experts. Some content features people who are described as experts but have no relevant qualifications, or real experts speaking about topics outside their field.
A famous example

One of the best-known examples of a false story spreading widely happened during a national election. A website that looked like a local newspaper published a story claiming that a famous religious leader had endorsed one of the candidates. The website was not a real newspaper, the leader had never said anything of the kind, and there were no named sources in the article. Despite being completely false, the story was shared millions of times. Many people who shared it never clicked on the link at all. They simply saw the headline, felt that it confirmed what they already believed, and passed it on. When journalists later investigated, they discovered that the website had been created by people who were not interested in politics at all. They were interested in money. Every click on their website earned them income from advertisements. The more shocking the story, the more clicks they received. For them, the truth was simply not part of the business model.
A practical checklist
How can you protect yourself? You do not need to become a professional fact-checker. A few simple habits can make a big difference.
First, pause. If a story makes you feel very angry, frightened, or excited, that is a signal to slow down. Strong emotions are exactly what misleading content is designed to produce.

Second, check the source. Who published this? Is it a well-known news organization with a reputation for accuracy, or a website you have never heard of? Ask yourself whether the source is reliable. Look at the website address carefully. Some fake sites copy the design and name of real news organizations, with small changes in the address.

Third, read beyond the headline. Many people share articles after reading only the headline. Often the article itself is more careful, or even says something different from what the headline suggests.

Fourth, look for other sources. If a story is true and important, other reliable news organizations will probably be reporting it too. If you cannot find it anywhere else, be cautious. This technique, which professional fact-checkers call "lateral reading," means leaving the page and checking what other sources say about the claim and about the website itself.
Fifth, check the date. Old stories are often shared again as if they were new, which can be very misleading.

Sixth, consider the evidence. Does the article include evidence, such as named sources, data, documents, or quotes from people with direct knowledge? Or does it rely on vague claims and emotional language?
Finally, when in doubt, do not share. Sharing a false story, even with good intentions, helps it spread. It is better to wait and check than to spread something false.
The difference between fact and opinion

Another important skill is distinguishing facts from opinions. A fact is a statement that can be checked and proven true or false, such as "The unemployment rate fell last month." An opinion is a personal judgment, such as "The government's economic policy is a disaster." Opinions are not bad. Newspapers have opinion sections, and thoughtful opinions can help us understand complex issues. But it is important to recognize when you are reading an opinion, and not to confuse it with a factual report.

Similarly, every news organization and every journalist has some bias, some perspective that influences what stories they choose and how they tell them. Recognizing bias does not mean that all sources are equally unreliable. Some organizations have strong standards for checking facts and correcting mistakes, and others do not. A good strategy is to get news from several reliable sources with different perspectives.
Thinking clearly in a confusing world

Critical thinking does not mean believing nothing. It means believing things for good reasons, and being willing to change your mind when you find better evidence. It means asking questions: How do we know this? What is the evidence? Who benefits if I believe this? What would change my mind?

It also means being humble. Despite being very careful, we will all sometimes believe something false. When that happens, the best response is not to defend the mistake, but to correct it. Admitting "I was wrong about that" is not a weakness. It is a sign of a mind that values truth more than pride.

In the end, the health of our information environment depends on all of us. Every time we stop to check a story before sharing it, every time we read beyond the headline, and every time we listen respectfully to someone who disagrees with us, we make the world a little more truthful. In an age of shark photos on flooded highways, that is no small thing.
